name: Rem Koolhaas
bio: Koolhaas began as a journalist and screenwriter, and wrote Delirious New York — a retroactive manifesto for Manhattan — before he had built anything at all. The office he co-founded, OMA, became a machine for turning research into buildings and buildings into arguments, with a mirror-image think tank, AMO, for the arguments that never needed walls. CCTV bent the skyscraper into a loop; Seattle turned a library into a stacked diagram of its own program; S,M,L,XL made the monograph into a cultural object. Half the leading offices of the last thirty years — Zaha Hadid, MVRDV, BIG, and the rest of the diaspora — passed through his; no architect since Le Corbusier has supplied the discipline with more of its vocabulary.

projects.title: CCTV Headquarters
projects.blurb: A looped skyscraper that swaps the race for height for a question about form.

projects.title: Seattle Central Library
projects.blurb: A stack of programmatic platforms wrapped in a diagrid skin.

projects.title: Casa da Música
projects.blurb: A faceted white boulder with a shoebox hall carved through it.

projects.title: Maison à Bordeaux
projects.blurb: A house whose center is a room-sized elevator, built for a client in a wheelchair.

projects.title: Kunsthal
projects.blurb: A continuous spiraling circuit of ramps disguised as a simple box.

projects.title: Fondazione Prada
projects.blurb: A distillery campus with a gold-leafed haunted house and a mirrored tower.

projects.title: Educatorium
projects.blurb: A folded floor becoming wall becoming roof for a university.

projects.title: Villa dall'Ava
projects.blurb: A glass house with a lap pool on the roof aimed at the Eiffel Tower.

projects.title: Nederlands Dans Theater
projects.blurb: The early low-budget masterwork of found materials and invention (demolished 2016).

projects.title: Qatar National Library
projects.blurb: A single lifted plate where all the books are visible at once.

name: Bernard Tschumi
bio: Son of the architect Jean Tschumi, born in Lausanne in 1944 and trained at ETH Zurich, Tschumi spent the 1970s teaching at the AA in London, arguing — with drawings, film frames and the occasional advertisement — that architecture has no meaning without the events that happen inside it. The Manhattan Transcripts made him theory's favorite architect; the 1983 competition for Parc de la Villette, won over some 470 entries including one from OMA, made the theory concrete as a grid of red steel folies across a former slaughterhouse district. As dean of Columbia's GSAPP from 1988 to 2003 he steered an entire school toward the digital while building concert halls, campuses and factories of his own. The Acropolis Museum in Athens, its top gallery rotated to face the Parthenon, keeps a floor ready for marbles still in London — the polemicist's building to the last.

projects.title: Parc de la Villette
projects.blurb: Twenty-six red steel folies on a strict grid over former slaughterhouses — the competition win that made deconstruction buildable.

projects.title: Acropolis Museum
projects.blurb: A concrete-and-glass museum whose top gallery twists to align with the Parthenon, holding space for the marbles London retains.

projects.title: Le Fresnoy Art Center
projects.blurb: A vast electronic roof floated over a 1920s leisure palace, with the in-between space left as found.

projects.title: The Manhattan Transcripts
projects.blurb: Theoretical drawings notating spaces together with the movements and events inside them; the built work's founding document.

projects.title: Alfred Lerner Hall
projects.blurb: Columbia's student center — glass ramps suspended between two masonry wings that keep the campus grid.

projects.title: Zénith de Rouen
projects.blurb: A 7,000-seat concert hall wrapped in a torqued metal envelope on the city's edge.

projects.title: Paris Zoological Park
projects.blurb: The Vincennes zoo rebuilt as immersive biozones around its 1930s artificial Great Rock.

projects.title: Vacheron Constantin Headquarters
projects.blurb: A single folded metal skin curling over workshops and offices for the watchmaker.

projects.title: MuséoParc Alésia
projects.blurb: A cylindrical interpretive center ringed in timber lattice on the presumed site of Caesar's victory over Vercingetorix.

projects.title: Blue Condominium
projects.blurb: A pixelated blue-glass tower cantilevering over its Lower East Side tenement neighbors.

name: Thom Mayne
bio: Dismissed from the architecture faculty at Cal Poly Pomona in 1972, Mayne co-founded both Morphosis and, with the other exiles, SCI-Arc — a school without walls conceived as an institutional rebuke — in the same year. For two decades the office survived on Los Angeles houses and restaurants, Kate Mantilini on Wilshire chief among them, developing a language of layered steel, tilted planes and machinery worn on the outside. Diamond Ranch High School proved the aggression could serve a public school on a public budget, and the federal Design Excellence program then handed him courthouses and headquarters, including a San Francisco tower that ventilates itself without air conditioning. The Pritzker came in 2005, to an architect who had played the combatant so long that respectability seemed the greater provocation; he has spent it on ever-larger civic work and on urban research at UCLA.

projects.title: Diamond Ranch High School
projects.blurb: A public high school as an inhabited canyon, its folded metal roofs negotiating a steep unbuildable site.

projects.title: San Francisco Federal Building
projects.blurb: A thin perforated-steel slab that ventilates naturally — a federal tower without air conditioning.

projects.title: Caltrans District 7 Headquarters
projects.blurb: A brooding downtown block for the highway agency, skinned in perforated aluminum panels that open and close with the sun.

projects.title: 41 Cooper Square
projects.blurb: Cooper Union's academic building — a torn steel veil around a full-height social stair.

projects.title: Perot Museum of Nature and Science
projects.blurb: A striated concrete cube with a glass escalator tube crawling up its face.
projects.wikipedia: Perot Museum of Nature and Science

projects.title: Wayne L. Morse United States Courthouse
projects.blurb: Ribbons of stainless steel folding over the courtrooms of a small Oregon city.
projects.wikipedia: Wayne L. Morse United States Courthouse

projects.title: Kate Mantilini
projects.blurb: A steakhouse as built manifesto — an exposed steel armature crashing through a Wilshire storefront (closed 2014).

projects.title: Emerson College Los Angeles

projects.title: Bill & Melinda Gates Hall

projects.title: Hanking Center
projects.blurb: A 350-meter tower with its core pulled outside the body — the diagram made vertical.

name: Jean Nouvel
bio: The son of two teachers from Fumel, Nouvel failed to convince his parents that painting was a career, took first place in the entrance exam to the École des Beaux-Arts instead, and by twenty was running projects for Claude Parent and Paul Virilio. He co-founded the Mars 1976 movement and the Syndicat de l'Architecture to fight the French architectural establishment, then joined it at a stroke in 1987 when the Institut du Monde Arabe opened with a south wall of mechanical diaphragms dilating like camera lenses. He has refused a signature ever since, insisting each building be a specific object distilled from its place: a dematerialized glass veil in Paris, a blue steel void in Minneapolis, a desert rose of colliding discs in Doha, a rain of light beneath the Louvre Abu Dhabi's dome. The Pritzker arrived in 2008; the buildings, in every conceivable shape, have not stopped since.

projects.title: Institut du Monde Arabe
projects.blurb: A south facade of 240 mechanical diaphragms modulating light like camera apertures — the building that made his name at 42.

projects.title: Louvre Abu Dhabi
projects.blurb: A 180-meter perforated dome dropping a 'rain of light' over a museum-city of white galleries.

projects.title: Fondation Cartier
projects.blurb: Layered glass screens that dissolve the boundary between building, garden and boulevard.

projects.title: Torre Agbar
projects.blurb: A shimmering projectile-shaped tower in 4,500 colored louvers, now Torre Glòries.

projects.title: Philharmonie de Paris
projects.blurb: A hill of interlocking aluminum birds concealing one of the great surround concert halls — opened late, over budget, and to acclaim.

projects.title: Musée du quai Branly
projects.blurb: A museum for non-Western art raised on pilotis behind a living green wall by the Seine.
projects.wikipedia: Musée du quai Branly – Jacques Chirac

projects.title: National Museum of Qatar
projects.blurb: Hundreds of sand-colored discs colliding like a desert rose around the old emiri palace.

projects.title: KKL Luzern
projects.blurb: A culture and congress center under a colossal flat roof cantilevering over the lake's edge.

projects.title: Guthrie Theater
projects.blurb: A midnight-blue theater complex with an 'endless bridge' lobby cantilevered toward the Mississippi.

projects.title: One Central Park
projects.blurb: Residential towers in vertical gardens by Patrick Blanc, with a heliostat throwing sunlight into the shadows.

name: Daniel Libeskind
bio: Born in Łódź in 1946 to Holocaust survivors, Libeskind came to New York in 1959 as a teenage accordion virtuoso, his passage aided by an America-Israel Cultural Foundation scholarship awarded alongside the young Itzhak Perlman. He studied at Cooper Union, then spent three decades as a nomadic theorist whose drawings — the Micromegas, the Chamber Works — were far better known than any building. His first, the Felix Nussbaum Haus, opened when he was 52; the Jewish Museum Berlin followed in 2001, a zigzag of slashed zinc threaded with voids that drew 350,000 visitors while still completely empty. Museums of memory and catastrophe followed worldwide, along with the 2003 master plan for Ground Zero — won in public, diluted in committee, but still governing the site's spiral of towers.

projects.title: Jewish Museum Berlin
projects.blurb: A zinc zigzag cut with window-wounds and threaded with voids; it drew hundreds of thousands before a single exhibit was installed.

projects.title: Imperial War Museum North
projects.blurb: A globe shattered into three shards — earth, air and water — reassembled as a museum of conflict.

projects.title: World Trade Center Master Plan
projects.blurb: The Ground Zero plan won in open competition: a descending spiral of towers around the memorial voids.

projects.title: Royal Ontario Museum Crystal
projects.blurb: The Michael Lee-Chin Crystal — prismatic aluminum shards erupting from a Beaux-Arts museum onto Bloor Street.

projects.title: Denver Art Museum, Hamilton Building
projects.blurb: Titanium peaks angled at the Rockies; his first completed building in the United States.

projects.title: Felix Nussbaum Haus
projects.blurb: A museum for a painter murdered at Auschwitz, its narrowing corridors built to unsettle; Libeskind's first building.

projects.title: Bundeswehr Military History Museum
projects.blurb: A steel wedge driven through a nineteenth-century arsenal, pointing toward the source of the 1945 firebombing.

projects.title: Contemporary Jewish Museum
projects.blurb: A blue-steel cube derived from the Hebrew letters of 'l'chaim', tipped into a landmarked power substation.

projects.title: Bord Gáis Energy Theatre
projects.blurb: A 2,000-seat theater behind a tilted glass proscenium on the regenerated Grand Canal Dock.

projects.title: Reflections at Keppel Bay
projects.blurb: Six curving glass towers leaning in pairs over a former shipyard harbor.

name: Steven Holl
bio: Holl grew up in Bremerton, Washington, across the Sound from Seattle, and has kept something Pacific-Northwestern — light, water, mist — at the center of a New York practice founded in 1977. Every project begins the same way: a small watercolor painted at dawn, hundreds a year, from which the concept must survive translation into concrete and glass. His alliance with the Finnish phenomenologists made experience itself the program — how light falls, how a ramp sounds underfoot — and Kiasma in Helsinki, won over local grumbling that an American had taken Finland's museum, proved the method at civic scale. Simmons Hall gave MIT a porous concrete sponge of a dormitory; the Bloch Building gave the Nelson-Atkins five glowing glass lenses in a lawn. He has taught at Columbia since 1981 and remains the discipline's most persistent argument that a building is something you feel before you understand.

projects.title: Kiasma
projects.blurb: Finland's museum of contemporary art — two intertwining volumes tuned to the low northern light.

projects.title: Bloch Building, Nelson-Atkins Museum
projects.blurb: Five translucent glass 'lenses' stepping down a sculpture lawn, glowing like lanterns at night.

projects.title: Chapel of St. Ignatius
projects.blurb: Seven 'bottles of light' — colored volumes gathered on a tilt-up concrete box for a Jesuit campus.

projects.title: Linked Hybrid
projects.blurb: Eight towers joined by a ring of skybridges — a porous, public alternative to the gated compound.

projects.title: Simmons Hall
projects.blurb: An MIT dormitory as a porous sponge, ten stories of 5,500 small square windows.

projects.title: Hunters Point Community Library
projects.blurb: A slim concrete slab on the East River, carved open toward the Manhattan skyline.

projects.title: Reid Building, Glasgow School of Art
projects.blurb: A pale glass counterpoint facing Mackintosh's masterwork, with driven voids pulling light down through the studios.

projects.title: Stretto House
projects.blurb: A house composed like Bartók's music — heavy masonry bars overlapped by curving light rooms across a creek.

projects.title: Storefront for Art and Architecture
projects.blurb: With Vito Acconci: a gallery facade of pivoting panels that abolishes its own wall when open.

projects.title: The REACH, Kennedy Center
projects.blurb: Three white concrete pavilions folded into a landscape beside the marble box, for rehearsal and education.

name: John Pawson
bio: Pawson reached architecture through the back door: born into a Halifax textile family in 1949, he worked in the family mill, drifted to Japan to teach English, and gravitated to the Tokyo studio of Shiro Kuramata, who told him to go home and study. He enrolled at the AA at thirty, left without completing the course, and in 1981 opened a studio that has spent four decades subtracting. The Calvin Klein flagship on Madison Avenue made his emptiness fashionable in 1995; the Cistercian monks of Sept-Fons, recognizing a familiar austerity in it, commissioned the monastery of Nový Dvůr — the job he had, in effect, been rehearsing all along. His book Minimum gave the approach a theory of essentials, and the Design Museum's 2016 move into the old Commonwealth Institute gave it a public building. He remains the rare architect whose rooms are famous for what has been left out of them.

projects.title: Nový Dvůr Monastery
projects.blurb: A Cistercian monastery in white plaster and light, commissioned by monks who saw their own austerity in his shops.

projects.title: Design Museum
projects.blurb: The listed Commonwealth Institute and its hyperbolic-paraboloid roof remade as a calm oak-lined interior for design.

projects.title: Calvin Klein Collections Store
projects.blurb: A Madison Avenue bank stripped to stone, light and almost nothing else — minimalism's retail landmark.

projects.title: Sackler Crossing
projects.blurb: A black granite bridge curving flush with the lake surface at Kew Gardens.

projects.title: St Moritz Church
projects.blurb: A thousand-year-old church pared back to white surfaces and veiled onyx light.

projects.title: Neuendorf House
projects.blurb: With Claudio Silvestrin: a terracotta-pigmented wall in an almond grove, entered through a single tall slot.

projects.title: Pawson House
projects.blurb: His own Notting Hill terrace house gutted to a test bed for the life of almost nothing.

projects.title: Life House
projects.blurb: A Welsh holiday house for Alain de Botton's Living Architecture, planned around rituals of retreat.

projects.title: Baron House
projects.blurb: A Swedish farmhouse plan redrawn as four white wings around a courtyard of prevailing wind and light.

projects.title: The Jaffa
projects.blurb: A nineteenth-century convent and hospital in Old Jaffa converted into a hotel of bare stone and shadow.

name: Zaha Hadid
bio: Born in Baghdad and trained at the AA in London under Koolhaas and Zenghelis, Hadid spent her first two decades as the most famous unbuilt architect alive, winning competitions — most bitterly the Cardiff Bay Opera House — that a skeptical establishment declined to construct. Her early paintings, all suprematist shards and impossible gravity, turned out to be working drawings for a career: when the Vitra Fire Station finally rose in 1993, the fragments stood up. The buildings that followed traded shards for fluid, continuous surfaces, and made her the first woman to win the Pritzker Prize. By her sudden death in 2016 the practice was global, the geometry had a name — parametricism — and the field's center of gravity had permanently shifted.

projects.title: Vitra Fire Station
projects.blurb: Her first building — frozen movement in tilted concrete planes.

projects.title: MAXXI
projects.blurb: A museum of flowing concrete ribbons; the Stirling Prize winner that announced her mature phase.

projects.title: Heydar Aliyev Center
projects.blurb: A single continuous surface folding from plaza to roof, without a straight line in sight.

projects.title: London Aquatics Centre
projects.blurb: A wave-shaped roof over the 2012 Olympic pools.

projects.title: Guangzhou Opera House
projects.blurb: Twin boulders on the Pearl River, eroded by imagined water.

projects.title: Phaeno Science Centre
projects.blurb: A crater-legged concrete landscape you walk beneath.

projects.title: Bergisel Ski Jump
projects.blurb: Part tower, part bridge — a piece of athletic infrastructure as sculpture.

projects.title: Riverside Museum
projects.blurb: A pleated zinc section extruded from city to river.

projects.title: Rosenthal Center
projects.blurb: The first American museum designed by a woman; an urban carpet pulling the street inside.

projects.title: Morpheus Hotel
projects.blurb: An exoskeletal tower carved through with voids, completed after her death.

name: Herzog & de Meuron
bio: Jacques Herzog and Pierre de Meuron, both born in Basel in 1950, met in primary school, studied under Aldo Rossi at ETH Zurich, and founded their partnership in 1978 a few streets from where they grew up. The early work was almost mute — a copper-banded signal box, a Ricola warehouse of stacked timber slats — and made ornament respectable again by treating a building's skin as its entire argument. Tate Modern's conversion of Bankside power station made them global in 2000, the Pritzker followed in 2001, and Beijing's bird's-nest stadium, conceived with Ai Weiwei, became the most photographed structure of its decade. They have refused a house style with unusual discipline: each project gets a fresh material experiment — gabion walls, printed glass, pillowed ETFE — run from a Basel office that remains their laboratory. Artists have been collaborators throughout, which may explain why the buildings behave less like objects than like images you can enter.

projects.title: Tate Modern
projects.blurb: Bankside power station turned art museum, its Turbine Hall a covered public square; the twisted-brick Switch House followed in 2016.

projects.title: Beijing National Stadium
projects.blurb: The Olympic bird's nest — structure and ornament fused into one steel thicket, with Ai Weiwei consulting.

projects.title: Elbphilharmonie
projects.blurb: A glass wave of a concert hall on a harbor warehouse — a decade late, wildly over budget, instantly the city's emblem.

projects.title: Allianz Arena
projects.blurb: A stadium wrapped in inflated ETFE pillows that glow in the home team's colors.

projects.title: de Young Museum
projects.blurb: A copper-mesh museum in Golden Gate Park, perforated to dapple like tree canopy and left to oxidize green.

projects.title: Dominus Winery
projects.blurb: A long dark bar of gabion walls — loose basalt in wire cages — moderating the Napa climate without machinery.

projects.title: Prada Aoyama
projects.blurb: A crystalline six-story flagship whose diamond-grid structure is also its facade and its display case.

projects.title: CaixaForum Madrid
projects.blurb: A brick power station sliced free of its base and floated above the street, crowned in rusted cast iron.

projects.title: M+
projects.blurb: An inverted-T museum of visual culture on Victoria Harbour, its facade doubling as a giant LED screen.

projects.title: 1111 Lincoln Road
projects.blurb: A parking garage as open concrete shelving, hosting shops, parties and weddings between the cars.

name: Santiago Calatrava
bio: Calatrava trained as an architect in Valencia, then took a doctorate in civil engineering at ETH Zurich, and has spent a career insisting the two disciplines are one — preferably expressed in white steel, preferably suggesting motion. Bridges made his name in the late 1980s: the Alamillo in Seville, a harp leaning against the sky, established the tilted-pylon silhouette that cities began commissioning like a signature dish. Stations in Zurich, Lisbon and Liège turned engineering into public theater, and the City of Arts and Sciences remade his hometown's dry riverbed into a gleaming skeletal acropolis. He is also the profession's standing cautionary tale on budgets — Valencia pursued him over an opera house shedding its tiles, and New York's Oculus opened years late at roughly four billion dollars, the most expensive station ever built. The public, meanwhile, keeps coming; few architects since Gaudí have made structure so frankly emotional.

projects.title: City of Arts and Sciences
projects.blurb: An opera house, science museum, planetarium and arboretum as white skeletal organisms in the Turia's old riverbed.

projects.title: Milwaukee Art Museum
projects.blurb: The Quadracci Pavilion's brise-soleil — 66-meter wings that open and close over Lake Michigan — his first US building.

projects.title: World Trade Center Transportation Hub
projects.blurb: The Oculus — a ribbed white dove released at Ground Zero, and the most expensive station ever built.

projects.title: Turning Torso
projects.blurb: A residential tower twisting 90 degrees over nine stacked cubes, from his own sculpture of a rotating spine.

projects.title: Alamillo Bridge
projects.blurb: A single 142-meter pylon leaning back like a harp, holding the deck with no back-stays — bravado as statics.

projects.title: Stadelhofen Station
projects.blurb: A hillside commuter station threaded with ribbed concrete undercrofts and steel pergolas; the early masterwork.

projects.title: Gare do Oriente
projects.blurb: A glass-and-steel forest of Gothic palms over the platforms, built for Expo '98.

projects.title: Liège-Guillemins Station
projects.blurb: A 200-meter arched canopy of steel and glass dissolving the boundary between station and city.

projects.title: Auditorio de Tenerife

projects.title: Athens Olympic Sports Complex
